name: Colin Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Colin. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We've no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and everything here is confidential. What does a normal day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm head of the arable and the calf rearing at Hartley's, which is a dairy and arable farm, about 300 hectares. The milking's done by another team, I look after the calves from day one to weaning, and I run all the cropping, wheat, barley, beans and grass for silage. Up at half five, calves first, they get fed before I do, then it's the fields till dark.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mr Hartley's a friend of my dad's from church, he took me on during uni for the summers and kept me on after. He's fair, but it's a family farm and the pay's not great, and I've got about three weeks of money in the bank. My girlfriend Ellie's a teaching assistant at the primary school, and we're saving for a few acres of our own one day, which at this rate is about the year 2060.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now maybe we can get back to farming. I'd probably say it after church, over coffee, half joking. I'm not big online, but I might share something on the farmers' group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't change much for me. I use a chatbot sometimes to check grain prices or write a letter to the bank, and that's handy, but I'm not counting on it. The real problem is still my pay and the price of land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. I'd keep doing hedge cutting for a couple of neighbours in winter, cash in hand, which is about four hundred extra a month in a good month. And I'd keep putting a bit by for the land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Steady, like a good day's drilling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The hedge cutting. Does Mr Hartley mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, he lends me the flail if I give him a cut of it. That's how farming round here works: one man's tractor, another man's hedge, and a bit of cash between friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Saving for land with three weeks in the bank. How do you think about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slowly. Ellie says I'm an optimist. I'd rather be an optimist with a plan than sit around moaning about house prices.

S0.say: I'd say good, now maybe we can get back to farming, half joking over coffee after church. I might share something on the farmers' group.
S0.think: It doesn't change much for me, because I only use a chatbot now and then for grain prices and letters. My real problem is still pay and the price of land.
S0.do: Keeps doing winter hedge cutting for neighbours, about four hundred a month in a good month. Keeps putting a little by towards buying a few acres.
S0.quote: That's how farming round here works: one man's tractor, another man's hedge, and a bit of cash between friends.
S0.fieldNote: He has a cheerful, can-do manner and a strong sense of local give-and-take. His side income from hedge cutting shows how he copes with low pay. Land ownership is his long-term goal, even if he jokes about the timescale.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Right, next one. This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it'll sort out the good farms from the lazy ones, and that's not all bad. But I'd also say the government shouldn't make it harder with endless forms and rules for small farms. I'd say that at the young farmers' meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's mostly okay for me if I keep up. The calf side needs hands, and somebody has to run the crop kit. But if Hartley's goes for a robot calf feeder and a self-driving sprayer, I'd need to show I can run them, or I'm the one who's surplus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait to see the kit working on a couple of farms round here, then I'd go on the training days the dealers run. I'd ask Mr Hartley to let me trial the calf feeder in the second year. And we'd keep saving, maybe push it up a bit, a hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not losing sleep, just keeping one eye on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the government shouldn't make it harder. Harder how?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every time there's something new, there's a grant you can only get if you fill in forty pages. The big farms have an office girl for the forms, and the small ones have me at the kitchen table at midnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about, at Hartley's?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Hartley himself, a bit. He's sixty-two and he doesn't like change any more than my dad does. If he digs in, the farm falls behind, and then we're all in trouble.

S1.say: I'd say it'll sort the good farms from the lazy ones, which isn't all bad. The government shouldn't make it harder for small farms with endless forms and rules.
S1.think: It's mostly okay for me if I keep up, because the calves need hands and someone runs the crop kit. But if the farm buys a robot calf feeder and a self-driving sprayer, I need to run them or I'm surplus.
S1.do: Waits to see new kit working on a couple of local farms, then goes on dealer training days. Asks the owner to trial a robot calf feeder in the second year and raises his saving to a hundred a month.
S1.feel: Uneasy, keeping one eye on it without losing sleep.
S1.quote: The big farms have an office girl for the forms, and the small ones have me at the kitchen table at midnight.
S1.fieldNote: He's steady: open to new kit but only once neighbours have tested it. His frustration is with paperwork and government rules that favour big farms. His concern for the owner's resistance to change shows he sees risk in standing still too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now three bigger ones. This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness, and that whoever's letting it happen hasn't thought about ordinary people. I'd say farming families are going to be wiped out. And I'd say we need to look after our own, because I'm not sure anybody else will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think Hartley's would be sold or turned over to machines, and I'd be out in a year or so. The land dream's gone. With three weeks of money, I'd be relying on family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd stop saving for land and put everything into a rainy day pot. I'd take every bit of hedge and fencing work going while people still pay a man to do it. Once it arrives, Ellie and I would probably move in with my parents on their smallholding, and I'd help Dad with his sheep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like a cow that's down and won't get up, you know it's bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning give you, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not enough to retrain, but enough to get my house in order. Two years is enough time to pay off the van, and that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You talked about looking after your own. What would you say to Ellie about your plans together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've talked about getting married, no date set, maybe next year. I'd say let's do it anyway, small, in the chapel. If everything's going to change, I'd rather face it married.

S2.say: I'd say it's madness, and whoever's letting it happen hasn't thought about ordinary people. Farming families will be wiped out, so we need to look after our own.
S2.think: I think the farm would be sold or handed to machines, and I'd be out within a year or so. The land dream is gone, and with three weeks of money I'd rely on family.
S2.do: Stops saving for land and builds a rainy-day pot instead, taking every hedge and fencing job he can. Moves with his girlfriend to his parents' smallholding once AGI arrives and helps with his father's sheep, and plans a small chapel wedding.
S2.feel: Alarmed, like a cow that's down and won't get up.
S2.quote: Two years is enough time to pay off the van, and that's about it.
S2.fieldNote: He turns quickly from his usual optimism to looking after family and community. He blames those letting it happen, not the farm owner. The decision to marry sooner and small is a revealing response to uncertainty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, a bit slower. This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if people stop moaning and start learning. And I'd say firms should take on apprentices to fix and run the machines, not just hire graduates from the city. I'd say that loudly at the young farmers'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gives me a shot. I'm good with machines and I've got the degree. If I can get into agricultural engineering, fixing the robots, I've got a few good years and maybe a skill that lasts a bit longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd apply for the agricultural engineering apprenticeship at the dealer in town, even if it's less money at first. I'd keep the hedge cutting going to cover the gap. And I'd use the AI tools more, properly, to learn how they think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a useful way. I'd have a job to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Less money at first, with three weeks of savings. How would that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight. Ellie's wage would carry the rent and mine would cover the van and food. I'd be a twenty-eight-year-old apprentice, which my dad would find very funny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you between two years and five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two, I'm running home. With five I can actually learn something new and earn from it before it all lands. That's a big difference.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough if people stop moaning and start learning. Firms should take on apprentices to run and fix the machines, not just city graduates.
S3.think: Five years gives me a shot, because I'm good with machines and I have the degree. If I get into agricultural engineering I've got a few good years and a skill that lasts longer.
S3.do: Applies for an agricultural engineering apprenticeship at the local dealer in the first year, accepting lower pay, and keeps hedge cutting to cover the gap. Uses AI tools more seriously to learn how they work.
S3.feel: Anxious, but in a useful way.
S3.quote: I'd be a twenty-eight-year-old apprentice, which my dad would find very funny.
S3.fieldNote: The middle timeline lets him act on his belief in apprenticeships, applying it to himself. He'd take a pay cut and rely on his girlfriend's wage for a while. He's not embarrassed to start again, only aware his father would tease him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair bit of time, so let's be sensible. Train people up, keep land with farming families, and don't let the government smother it in red tape. That's what I'd say over coffee after church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years might be good for me, if I use it right. I'd be thirty-seven. I could learn the kit, work for a few years fixing it, save, and maybe buy those few acres when prices drop because the big farms are all automated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Hartley's for the next couple of years and push for the calf feeder trial. I'd start the engineering apprenticeship in year two or three. And Ellie and I would get married next year, and keep saving, a bit more each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more hopeful than not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said land prices might drop. Is that a real hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've no idea, honestly, I'm guessing. But if nobody needs farm workers, nobody needs farm cottages either. Maybe the robots will finally make a few acres cheap enough for someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is long. Is there a risk you wait too long?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I'm not a jump-first person. But I'd rather go in a year late with my eyes open than first and blind. I'd keep an eye on the neighbours.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a fair bit of time, so be sensible: train people up, keep land with farming families and cut the red tape. I'd say it over coffee after church.
S4.think: Ten years might be good for me if I use it right. I could learn the kit, fix it for a few years, save, and maybe buy a few acres if prices drop.
S4.do: Stays at the farm for two years and pushes for the calf feeder trial, then starts an engineering apprenticeship in year two or three. Marries his girlfriend next year and saves a little more each year.
S4.feel: Uneasy but more hopeful than not.
S4.quote: Maybe the robots will finally make a few acres cheap enough for someone like me.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years he becomes hopeful, even imagining land getting cheaper, while admitting he's guessing. He keeps his steady style of watching neighbours before moving. His traditional views shape his wish list: training, family farms and less red tape.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time to learn anything and I'd be back at my dad's. What would help is proper paid apprenticeships for people already in farming, and less paperwork so small farms can actually get the grants. Give a farmer a trade, not a form, and he'll sort himself out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about community. The village hall, the church, the young farmers. If the farms empty out, there's nobody left to run any of it. That worries me more than the robots.

headlineQuote: Give a farmer a trade, not a form, and he'll sort himself out.
portrait: Colin Fischer is a 27-year-old who runs the arable side and calf rearing on a 300-hectare family dairy farm, with a degree, low pay, about three weeks of savings and a side line in winter hedge cutting, living with his girlfriend Ellie, a teaching assistant. He's traditional, church-going and cheerful, believes in apprenticeships and dislikes red tape, and uses AI tools now and then. If AI is hype he's calm, and steady change makes him uneasy but willing to train once neighbours have tried the kit. AGI in two years alarms him and sends him home to his parents' smallholding. With five or ten years he'd become an apprentice in farm machinery and still hopes to buy a few acres.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there's no time to learn anything and he'd be back at his father's.
whatWouldHelp: Paid apprenticeships for people already in farming and less paperwork so small farms can get grants.
